ResolveX

Making civic issue reporting more transparent and trackable.

Duration4 Weeks
Team2 Members
RoleUX Research · UI/UX Design
ToolsFigma, FigJam, Miro
01The Story

As a UX Researcher and Designer on a two-person team, I spent four weeks investigating why civic issue reporting felt like shouting into a void — and designed ResolveX to close that loop.

02Design Process
01

Research

Surveys and informal interviews on civic reporting habits.

02

Define

Framed the core problem as visibility, not just submission.

03

Ideate

Explored ways to make status and location effortless.

04

Wireframe

Sketched the reporting and tracking flows.

05

UI Design

Built the high-fidelity screens in Figma.

06

Prototype

Connected the flow for walkthroughs.

03The Problem

"Citizens can report civic issues, but often don't know what happens after they submit a complaint."

More on the problem

Reporting a pothole, a broken streetlight, or an overflowing bin rarely came with any visibility into what happened next — leaving citizens unsure whether anything was being done, and less likely to report the next issue they noticed.

05Discover

Research methods → findings → insight.

Primary research combined short surveys and informal interviews with people in and around campus and the neighbourhood about how they notice and report civic issues.

06What I Learned
Finding

Users struggle to know what happens after reporting.

Insight

The problem isn't only submission — it's a lack of visibility.

Decision

Create transparent status tracking, so every report has a visible life after it's sent.

12Final Experience

The high-fidelity flow, screen by screen — from the first open to a resolved, tracked complaint.

01 — Splash

Purpose in one glance

The logo and tagline, “Connecting citizens to faster solutions”, say what the app is for before it asks for anything.

02 — Onboarding 1: Report

Core action first

One illustration and one line show the main task. Log in, Sign up and “Continue as a guest” stay visible.

03 — Onboarding 2: Track

Answers the trust question

The second slide promises live progress, with a real status card so people see what tracking looks like.

04 — Onboarding 3: Community

Issues are shared

This slide introduces nearby reports. Language chips sit in the same place on every slide.

05 — Login

Phone-first, one main action

Only two fields. Log in is filled, Create account is outlined, and the guest link is plain text.

06 — Create account

Hints prevent errors

Five fields in one column, with short helper text under each so mistakes are fixed before submitting.

07 — Home

Key tasks near the top

Quick Report and Track Complaint come first, followed by nearby updates and local office performance.

08 — Report issue

Least effort first

Photo first, location detected automatically, category as icon tiles. Save Draft protects unfinished work.

09 — Submitted

Ends with certainty

A check mark, a copyable complaint ID, an estimated time and a three-step preview of what happens next.

10 — Complaint details

Progress you can follow

A six-stage timeline, plus the assigned department, contact person and location map, keeps the process accountable.

11 — Community issues

Map plus list

Colour-coded pins and a matching list show nearby issues, which also helps people avoid duplicate reports.

12 — Complaint resolved

Proof builds trust

Before and after photos show the work is done. Users then rate it and can leave feedback.

13 — Notifications

Updates come to you

Tabs separate updates from alerts. Each item names the complaint and its new status.

14 — Complaint history

Find any complaint fast

Search by ID or name, and filter by All, In Progress or Resolved.

15 — Profile

Everything else, one list

Photo and details at the top, then settings, saved reports, language and support in a single list.

16 — Help & Support

Self-help first

FAQs and How it works come first, with Chat with us placed lower on the screen.

13Outcome

From confusion to a clearer civic reporting experience

BeforeUnclear, slow and frustrating
  • Not sure where to report
  • Confusing process
  • No update after submission
  • Loss of trust
AfterSimple, transparent and trustworthy
Faster reportingSubmit a complaint in under a minute
Transparent trackingSee real-time status of your complaint
Improved trustKnow who is handling and what happens next
More civic engagementA simpler process encourages more people to report

This reflects the intended experience of the design concept, not a measured, deployed outcome — ResolveX was an academic case study, not a shipped product.

14Reflection
"Good civic tech isn't just about making reporting easy — it's about closing the loop."

Working with a partner on user research made me realise how much of the ResolveX problem was emotional, not just functional: people didn't stop reporting because the form was hard, they stopped because it felt like nothing happened after. That reframed the whole project around visibility and trust rather than just form design.

Campus Canteen App

Bitez

Making campus dining quicker, clearer, and easier to plan.

Duration4 Weeks
RoleUI/UX Designer
ToolsFigma, FigJam, Google Forms
TypeUX Case Study
01The Story

A 4-week solo case study into why ordering food on campus meant standing in line with no idea how long the wait would be — and designing a way around it.

02Design Process
01

Research

Looked at how students currently order and wait.

02

Define

Framed the core problem as queue time and visibility.

03

Ideate

Explored menu browsing and ordering ahead of time.

04

Wireframe

Sketched the home, menu, and cart flows.

05

UI Design

Built the high-fidelity ordering screens.

06

Prototype

Connected the ordering-to-tracking flow.

03The Problem

Long queues and a manual ordering process made campus dining slow — with no way to track an order once it was placed.

More on the problem

Beyond the wait itself, the canteen menu wasn't easy to browse ahead of time, so most of the delay came from deciding and ordering at the counter rather than the cooking itself.

04User Interviews

Primary research with students and canteen staff surfaced five recurring themes.

Current Flow & Time

Students feel rushed, stressed, and often late for classes due to canteen delays.

Payment Friction

Slow payment processes (cash, GPay) and unsanitary concerns with cash handling.

Order Status Chaos

Missed orders, confusion, and shouting create an aggressive environment.

App Adoption / Trust

Digital apps need to be reliable and guaranteed to earn student trust.

Staff Perspective

Staff struggle with no change, GPay fraud checks, and noise during rush hours.

05User Persona
V

"The canteen is my only option between lectures, but I often skip lunch entirely because the line is just too long to risk it."

Name
Varshini
Age
20
Role
2nd Year B.Tech (Computer Science & Engineering)
Location
Day Scholar (commutes 45 minutes to campus daily)
Tech Literacy
Power User — builds apps in her free time and expects digital efficiency in her physical environment

About

Varshini is a high-achiever with a rigorous course load. As a day scholar, she doesn't have a hostel room to retreat to, so the canteen is her primary "home base" during the day. She often carries a heavy laptop bag and needs a place to sit and recharge, both herself and her devices. She usually eats in a small group of 3–4 friends, and they try to coordinate their meals to save time.

Goals & Motivations

  • Nutritional transparency: wants to know ingredients or veg/non-veg status without interrogating a busy server.
  • Time budgeting: wants to "set and forget" an order so she can keep working while food is prepared.

Needs & Expectations

  • Remote ordering: place an order while walking from the library to the canteen.
  • Group ordering: see the total cost for her group to avoid "who owes what" math.
  • Digital receipts: prefers digital records over paper tokens for tracking expenses.

Pain Points

  • Physical inaccessibility: a crowded, first-come counter that feels frustrating and unprofessional.
  • The "shout" system: missed calls in a noisy canteen lead to cold food and more delays.

Personality

Patience
Extremely low
Tech reliance
Extremely high
Social energy
Moderate
Planning
High (pre-planner)
06Discover & Define
Finding

Long queues, limited menu visibility, and manual ordering made campus dining slow and frustrating.

Insight

Students needed to browse and order before reaching the counter, and know where their order stood while waiting.

Decision

Design a mobile ordering flow with clear categories, quick reordering, and real-time tracking.

07The Solution

The Smart Campus Canteen Ordering System enables students to browse menus, place orders remotely, track order status in real time, and receive pickup notifications through a mobile app.

The system reduces waiting times, eliminates pickup confusion, improves menu visibility, and creates a faster, more organized canteen experience.

11Final Experience

The high-fidelity flow, screen by screen — from first open to a tracked, paid order.

01 — Splash

A warm first impression

The Bitez wordmark sits on a warm orange gradient — a short, branded beat that sets the tone before the app gets functional.

02 — Onboarding

One screen, one message

Rather than a multi-step tutorial, a single illustrated screen communicates the app's value — ordering food, faster — with one clear "Get Started" action.

03 — Login

Low-friction access

Email and password sit above the fold, with Google and Facebook as one-tap alternatives — so returning students aren't slowed down before they can order.

04 — Home

Straight to the food

Search and meal-time filters (Breakfast, Lunch, Snacks) sit at the top, followed immediately by Recently Viewed and Popular Items — surfacing the fastest paths back to a familiar order.

05 — Categories

Browsing by mood, not just menu

The category panel groups the menu into a few plain-language buckets — Main Meals, Quick Bites, Drinks, Desserts — so browsing doesn't mean scrolling one long list.

06 — Search & Filter

Only what's actually ready

An "Available Now" filter, paired with veg/non-veg toggles, narrows results to items the canteen can serve immediately — directly addressing the original pickup-confusion problem.

07 — Order Details

Nothing hidden before paying

Each item shows its own price, prep time, and quantity control, with a running Payment Summary always visible — so the total at checkout is never a surprise.

08 — Checkout

Pay however is easiest

Google Pay sits alongside Cash on Pickup as equally prominent options, since not every student wants to pay digitally in advance for a same-day snack.

09 — Paid

A clear, calm confirmation

A single checkmark, the amount, and who it was paid to — confirming the order went through without adding any extra steps between paying and tracking.

10 — Order Tracking

Closing the original gap

A simple three-step status — Placed, Getting Prepared, Ready to Pickup — with an estimated pickup time. This is the direct answer to the "no way to track an order" problem from the start of the case study.

12Outcome

A simpler and more convenient campus dining experience

The new design makes ordering easier, gives clear updates, and creates a smoother dining experience for students.

BeforeConfusing and time-consuming
  • Long queues
  • Unclear menu
  • Manual payment
  • Crowded canteen
AfterEasy, clear and seamless
  • Quick ordering
  • Clear menu
  • Multiple payment options
  • Real-time order updates
Faster ordering
More transparency
Less crowd
Better experience

This reflects the intended experience of the design concept, not a measured, deployed outcome.

13Reflection
"Most of the wait wasn't cooking time — it was decision time."

This project taught me that a queue isn't just a physical problem; a lot of it is an information problem. Moving the menu-browsing and decision-making earlier in the journey did more for the experience than any change to the counter itself would have.

Study Material Organizer

One home for every resource.

Duration14 Days
RoleUI/UX Designer
ToolsFigma, FigJam, Google Forms
01The Story

A 14-day sprint to solve a problem every student already knows: notes, links, and recordings scattered across a dozen apps.

02Design Process
01

Research

Looked at where students currently keep materials.

02

Define

Framed the problem as fragmentation, not lack of tools.

03

Ideate

Explored centralizing and search-first navigation.

04

Wireframe

05

UI Design

03The Problem

Students store study materials across many platforms — making it hard to find, organize, or return to what they need when they need it.

04The Solution

A centralized platform that helps students collect, organize, and access study materials efficiently.

Smart search and auto-tagging automatically categorize notes, while integrated reminders and tasks support better study planning and reduce time spent searching for resources.

05User Journey

Following a student from receiving new material to revising for an exam — and how the frustration builds along the way.

🤔

User receives notes, links, PDFs

"Where did the teacher send the notes?" "Was it in WhatsApp or Google Classroom?"
Emotion: Confused
😣

Searching Materials (Multiple Platforms)

"I saved it somewhere..." "Was it in Drive or Downloads?"
Emotion: Frustrated
😫

Switching Between Apps

"I'm wasting my study time just searching." "Everything is scattered everywhere."
Emotion: Highly Frustrated
🤭

Finally Finding the Material

"Finally found it!" "That took so much time." "Now I'm already tired before studying."
Emotion: Tired / Relieved
😩

Exam / Revision Time

"Where are my revision notes?" "I saved so many links but can't find them." "This is so stressful before exams."
Emotion: Stressed
06Discover & Define
Finding

Materials were scattered across drives, chat apps, and notes tools, with no single place to search.

Insight

A single, searchable home for materials would cut the time spent hunting before actually studying.

Decision

Design a centralized organizer with smart search and lightweight productivity tools.

09Final Experience

The high-fidelity flow — from opening the app to scanning, saving, annotating, and staying on top of deadlines.

01 — Home

One home for every resource

Search, quick actions, and Recent Files all live on a single home screen — directly answering the original problem of materials being scattered with no central starting point.

02 — Search

Smart search, not another folder to dig through

Recent searches sit above Recent Files, so students can jump straight back to what they were looking for instead of re-typing or re-browsing every time.

03 — Add Material

Capture materials however they arrive

Camera, Videos, and Photos sit side by side as equal entry points, since study material rarely arrives in just one format — a photo of a whiteboard, a recorded lecture, or a printed handout.

04 — Scan

A guided, document-first capture

A clear alignment frame and a single capture action keep scanning fast — the thumbnail of the last page stays visible so a multi-page scan feels continuous.

05 — Select Pages

Built for more than one page

Numbered thumbnails and a Select All shortcut make it quick to gather an entire chapter or handout into one file instead of saving each page separately.

06 — Review & Edit

A chance to fix it before it's filed away

Edit, Crop, Share, and Save sit together as equal-weight actions, so cleaning up a crooked scan never feels like an extra detour.

07 — Save

Naming it well from the start

Asking for a file name at the moment of saving — rather than leaving everything as "Untitled" — is what makes smart search and auto-tagging actually work later.

08 — Saved

A clear, reassuring close

A single checkmark and file name confirm the save went through, with Share Document offered immediately for anyone who wants to send it on right away.

09 — Annotate

Studying happens on the material itself

Color, Pen, Text, and Eraser tools turn a saved scan into something to actively study from, instead of a flat file that just sits in storage.

10 — Reminders

Study planning lives next to study materials

Reminders sit under the same Updates tab as notifications, with completed tasks shown with a checkmark — keeping deadlines and materials in one connected space.

11 — Add Reminder

Flexible enough for real study habits

One-Time, Weekly, Daily, and Custom frequency options mean a reminder can match anything from a one-off submission to a recurring revision session.

12 — Notifications

Nothing gets missed

The Notification tab sits one tap away from Reminders, so a student never has to wonder whether an update about a deadline was seen or missed.

10Outcome

From scattered chaos to
an organized study space

Scattered and overwhelming

Hard to find files and notes

Plan and manage your learning

More productivity

Stay focused and track your progress

This reflects the intended experience of the design concept, not a measured, deployed outcome. Phone screens shown are from the design's high-fidelity flow.

11Reflection
"The fastest way to help someone study is to stop making them search."

Working within a tight 14-day timeline pushed me to prioritise ruthlessly — search and a single home for materials mattered far more than any extra feature, so that's what I designed first.
